newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl fenced in by Germany's restructuring woes.
newsitem.headline: Kohl fenced in by Germany's restructuring woes.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl is looking increasingly fenced in by his own consensus style of politics as he struggles to cut public spending and modernise Germany's economy to qualify for Europe's monetary union (EMU).

Proposals for subsidy cuts or shifts in economic policy are hardly floated these days before a chorus of pressure groups rises up in protest. Some ideas never even make it that far -- the politicians dare not suggest them.

Bonn's latest logjam -- a coal miners' protest that has paralysed the government quarter and locked the liberal Free Democrats out of their own headquarters -- vividly illustrates how narrow Kohl's room for manoeuvre has become.

On the one hand, his centre-right government took the bull by the horns in suggesting deep cuts in the nine billion mark ($5.3 billion) subsidies Bonn pays annually to keep producing coal at prices three times those on the well-stocked world market.

But the same leaders who approve using water cannon against anti-nuclear protesters or riot police against anarchists did nothing to stop a few thousand miners from turning the hub of Bonn into a camping ground.
They feared clashes with the miners, a small group with big political and physical clout.
"Now we have taboos like in the Third World," Munich's popular Abendzeitung remarked scornfully. "The Indians have their holy cows and we have our hellish lobbies."
Kohl's dilemma is easy to describe and hard to solve.

Record post-war unemployment of 4.7 million and economists' warnings that Bonn could miss the three percent budget deficit goal for EMU mean 1997 is the "make-or-break" year for hacking back the lush undergrowth of subsidies, tax breaks and public services that cushion Germany's extensive welfare state.
But that undergrowth also shores up a corporatist-style political system based on consensus and sharing out parts of a tasty pie of economic benefits.

With the pie now shrinking, both government and opposition politicians are torn between the general welfare and loudly clamouring special interest groups -- from striking coal or construction workers to powerful industrial lobbies.

"We are seeing a trend away from long-term political activity to spontaneous blockades," said political scientist Andreas Puettmann of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation, a think tank linked to Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU). "There is a danger that this could escalate."
Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung also saw the potential for more protests growing as Bonn proposes more spending cuts.
"The political struggles in this country will get worse. Other branches like construction have similar problems," it wrote in an editorial.
"The changes in Europe and wage differences between Germany and its eastern neighbours could lead to social upheavals which will make the miners' march look like a warning tremor."

The coal subsidies, which Kohl wants to slash from nine billion to 3.9 billion marks annually by 2005, are the latest issue ensnarled in the long and complex debates Bonn indulges in before a compromise emerges.

Kohl wanted a more generous compromise last autumn but critics in his own ranks -- CDU deputies from the rich south and the struggling east who cannot see why 90,000 coalminers in the west are so pampered -- sent him back to the drawing board.

The opposition Social Democrats are now holding up urgent talks on tax reform plans in protest against the unexpectedly tough coal proposal that would put half of today's pitworkers -- traditional SPD voters -- on the dole.
Kohl's coalition has yet to decide how to pursue an urgent pension reform, which links to the unfinished tax reform because competing models carry different price tags.
Independently of this, Health Minister Horst Seehofer is angering voters with health system reform plans that add up mostly to higher fees for patients.

"Kohl and his coalition share the blame that things could explode now," the Stuttgarter Zeitung wrote. "They have put off the inevitable for too long. That applies to coal, to taxes, to pensions, to health ... now it's all coming at once, and the euro too.

"Since Kohl has delayed so long, he has to demand an awful lot from people at once. They might present him with the bill for it on election day. That's the risk he faces. But he can't go back now." ($ = 1.708 German Marks)
